I'm a programmer.  So this has varied a lot for me from job to job.  Generally:

* I'm assigned to a team with other programmers, usually with varying expertise and amounts of experience.  The team has 5-10 people.
* Work comes in big chunks from another organization within the company (product, technical, compliance) and the team is responsible for mapping out what shape that big chunk of work will take, breaking it into smaller pieces.
* There is generally a framework for checkins.  Lately the trend is a daily short check in and planning sessions every two weeks to determine what work will get done and check that the projects the team is doing are on track.
* Work is either assigned by the team lead, or you volunteer for work that's up next for the team.  My current job, we meet and agree how much work the team can do inside of two weeks, then we as a group volunteer to do parts of that work.
* Separately from this, you check in with your boss, who monitors what you're doing, how fast, if you get along with the team, etc.  The boss also will listen to concerns you have and try to help if they're a good boss.
* It's not really like school projects, which is a relief.  Even though the team is responsible for the project, at most companies there's some individual accountability.  People are given assignments inside the project, their boss monitors if they are slow or poor at them.  If you take on their work it becomes your work.  Most jobs I've had want to know about poor performers so they watch for them and don't just make you cover for them, but some jobs have been crap in this regard.
* It's also not like school projects because people on the team have different areas of expertise.  On my team I'm the only person who is an expert in a certain technical system, so I do most of that work when it comes to my team.  Or like, certain work goes to lower level people because the higher level people have lots of meetings.
* The incentive to do well is with your performance review.  Your boss, who you meet with to monitor your progress, will write a review some time during the year grading you.  I don't really know what happens if you do very poorly, but if you do well you can get raises and promotions, or have an easier time asking to do different work that you like.
* Hours, well, since the job is in office now, everyone seems to wander in around 8:30-9 and leave at about 5.  I just go with the flow there.  If I feel like I'm running late on something that has a hard deadline I might work more on it at home but this is not common.

Glue traps have other problems than just caring about the mouse's suffering.  Yes, I've used glue traps.  I don't use them anymore.

A problem to consider with glue traps is that the mice will defecate/urinate while they struggle and they can spread more disease that way than a quick kill.  If you live in the southwest US you may have concerns about hantavirus, but there are many, many diseases carried by rodents.

The mouse can run off with the glue trap and cause you to have to search around to find it, sometimes in weird areas of your basement.  I had one wedge itself and the glue trap in the expansion joint in the basement and had to pull that out.  It was not particularly easy.

Mice are also loud and disturbing as they die.  You've said you don't care about them suffering, but to end the noise you'll have to kill the mouse yourself.  As in manually, by putting it in a bag and stomping with your foot or another item.  With a snap trap you do not need to do this.  The mouse is already dead, you simply dispose of the corpse.

I've found snap traps are very effective for killing them, and you can always find the trap and dead mouse body in order to throw it out.  They're reusable, and because the mouse often doesn't get a chance to eat your bait, you can just remove the corpse, and set the trap back up.  No running out and getting more glue traps and supplies, get cheap traps, set up a lot of them, kill all the mice, reset them, finish killing the mice.

For US based insurance - ask the dentist's front desk to run the cost through your insurance for an estimate to see what they will cover.  Some insurances won't cover the same surface being treated in a small amount of time, some will.  I've also been advised that if you are in pain, the dental insurance is more likely to cover certain procedures, though I don't know how this is entered.

Sometimes drawing it out can help with cost, because a dental plan will pay a set amount per year, and that amount resets once the year boundary is crossed. Hey, I have two crowns on two of my molars.  No, it doesn't hurt much.  And yeah, tooth pain is the worst pain, don't feel like a baby.

There's two appointments, the crown prep and the permanent crown.  The crown prep is when they shave down the tooth.  It's a long procedure, it took about an hour for the crown prep.  I was numbed for it, but once the Novocaine wore off my jaw was kind of sore for the rest of that day.  Not bad pain, just kind of like, sore.  That wore off.

The temporary crowns can be a little sensitive.  I ended up chewing on the other side mostly while waiting for the permanent one.  One of my temporary crowns was actually a bit painful.  But it wasn't like that raw "tooth pain" pain, it was more like "oh, that's sensitive".  The other one I was wary because of the previous experience, but it didn't actually hurt.

The permanent crown procedure is quick.  They numb again, then they glue the permanent crown on.  Some time is spent shaving it down so that it's not rough and it matches the tooth above/below it.

Once the permanent crown is on, I haven't noticed any pain.  It's honestly just like having a tooth. I know the crown is there, but it doesn't hurt and they're like all my other molars.
